action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation with chronic neurogenic change in bulbar, cervical and thoracic muscles and early in lumbosacral muscles; reduced CMAPs with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, hemorrhage, mass, demyelinating or enhancing lesion and a normal brainstem; subtle nonspecific corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the internal capsules is supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs, such as a brainstem tumour, infarct or demyelination in this bulbar-onset presentation; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Multilevel cervical spondylosis with C5-C6 canal stenosis but no cord compression or cord signal change; normal thoracic cord.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 748 U/L (4.4x ULN); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 72% predicted, SNIP 48 cmH2O, MIP -48 cmH2O and NIF -52 cmH2O are reduced; the MIP and NIF meet an AAN 2009 marker for NIV discussion.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic variant on the ALS gene panel; a negative result does not exclude a genetic contribution.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction with lisinopril, levothyroxine, calcium or vitamin D; baseline and scheduled transaminase monitoring with a stop threshold of ALT above 5x ULN, and a neutropenia warning.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. No current medicine interacts with it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not delay the swallowing assessment in a patient who is already choking or coughing on food or fluids.
Do not refer for cervical spine surgery on the basis of the C5-C6 spondylotic changes: they do not explain the bulbar signs or the denervation in other regions.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bulbar weakness spreading to the limbs with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, pseudobulbar affect, limb hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now and discuss NIV: MIP -48 cmH2O (NIF -52 cmH2O) meets an AAN 2009 marker of respiratory insufficiency; assess orthopnoea and overnight oximetry or capnography to time NIV, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.

Arrange a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment now (aspiration risk, safe food and fluid consistencies) and a dietetic review with baseline weight, and discuss gastrostomy early, while FVC is above 50% predicted.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Screen cognition and behaviour with a validated ALS tool (such as the ECAS), and explain the pseudobulbar affect (involuntary laughing or crying) to the patient and family, offering symptomatic treatment if it is distressing.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

differential.key_features: supports: multilevel cervical spondylosis with C5-C6 canal stenosis, limb hyperreflexia and Hoffman signs; against: no cord compression or cord signal change, bulbar signs (dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue atrophy and fasciculations, brisk jaw jerk) and denervation in tongue, thoracic paraspinal and lumbosacral muscles.

differential.diagnosis: Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN) with conduction block
differential.key_features: supports: asymmetric hand weakness with fasciculations; against: upper motor neuron signs, normal motor conduction velocities and no conduction block, bulbar involvement.
supports: dysarthria with nasal speech and dysphagia; against: no fatigable weakness or ocular signs, tongue atrophy and fasciculations, upper motor neuron signs and EMG denervation.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, pseudobulbar affect, limb hyperreflexia and bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions (bulbar-onset ALS phenotype).
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy.
CK 748 U/L (4.4x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

Respiratory function is already reduced (FVC 72% predicted, SNIP 48 cmH2O, MIP -48 cmH2O, NIF -52 cmH2O), and the MIP and NIF are weaker than -60 cmH2O. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).
Spondylotic changes are common at this age; they cannot explain the bulbar signs or the denervation in tongue, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.
Bulbar involvement carries a worse prognosis and an aspiration risk; swallowing assessment and early gastrostomy discussion, while FVC is above 50% predicted, are priorities.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Spondylosis is common at this age; there is no cord compression or cord signal change, and it cannot explain the bulbar signs (dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue atrophy and fasciculations, brisk jaw jerk) or the denervation in tongue, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles. It must not delay the ALS work-up.
red_herrings.data_point: Multilevel cervical spondylosis with C5-C6 central canal stenosis on spine MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on cervical myelopathy as the primary explanation, deferring the ALS work-up or prompting a neurosurgical referral

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Carpal tunnel syndrome was released 5 years ago. The current EMG shows active and chronic denervation in median-innervated (abductor pollicis brevis) and non-median muscles (first dorsal interosseous, extensor digitorum communis) of both arms and in other regions, with normal median sensory responses, which an entrapment neuropathy does not produce.
red_herrings.data_point: History of right carpal tunnel syndrome surgically released 5 years ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests entrapment neuropathy as the cause of current hand weakness

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.
Riluzole is considered only after the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment supports ALS.

findings.description: Disc desiccation at C5-C6 and C6-C7 with multilevel spondylotic change from C3-C4 to C6-C7. Moderate bilateral foraminal narrowing at C5-C6. Mild to moderate central canal stenosis at C5-C6 with CSF preserved around the cord. No intrinsic cord T2 signal change.
Normal thoracic cord signal and calibre. No disc protrusion, canal stenosis or intramedullary lesion.

body_imaging.impression: 1. Multilevel cervical spondylosis with mild to moderate C5-C6 central canal stenosis and moderate bilateral C5-C6 foraminal narrowing; no cord compression and no cord signal change. 2. Normal thoracic spinal cord.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal: CK 748 U/L (4.4x ULN). All other results are within reference ranges.

additional_observations: No significant cortical atrophy beyond age-expected
No white matter lesions to suggest demyelinating disease
No enhancing lesions on post-gadolinium sequences
Brainstem: no focal signal abnormality, normal size

findings.location: Posterior limbs of both internal capsules

mri.impression: 1. Subtle symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity along the corticospinal tracts in the posterior limbs of the internal capsules; nonspecific, may reflect corticospinal tract degeneration. 2. No infarct, hemorrhage, mass, demyelinating lesion or enhancing lesion. Normal brainstem.

findings.finding: Tongue: fibrillations +2, fasciculation potentials with complex morphology. Motor unit potentials: large amplitude (up to 2.5 mV), long duration, polyphasic. Reduced recruitment pattern with rapid firing of few units.

Right and left first dorsal interosseous, abductor pollicis brevis, extensor digitorum communis: fibrillations +1 to +2, positive sharp waves +1. Large amplitude MUPs with reduced recruitment. Fasciculation potentials present in biceps bilaterally.
T6-T8 paraspinal muscles: fibrillations +1 bilaterally. Sparse fasciculation potentials. Abnormal MUP morphology.
Right tibialis anterior: sparse fibrillations, positive sharp waves. Gastrocnemius: fasciculation potentials. Recruitment mildly reduced. Changes less prominent than upper body.

Median motor: CMAP amplitude 4.8 mV right, 3.9 mV left (mildly reduced); distal latency and conduction velocity normal. Ulnar motor: CMAP amplitude 3.2 mV left (reduced); conduction velocity 52 m/s (normal). Peroneal motor: CMAP amplitude 3.1 mV right (mildly reduced); conduction velocity 44 m/s. No conduction block identified.

Median sensory: SNAP amplitude 22 uV right, 20 uV left, normal. Ulnar sensory: SNAP amplitude 15 uV right, normal. Sural sensory: SNAP amplitude 18 uV right, normal. All sensory conduction velocities within normal limits.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves) and chronic reinnervation (large amplitude, long duration, polyphasic MUPs with reduced recruitment) in the bulbar, cervical and thoracic regions, with early lumbosacral involvement. 2. Reduced median, ulnar and peroneal CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. 3. Normal sensory nerve conduction studies. The findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells involving multiple body regions.

quantitative_data.dominant_emg_pattern: Active denervation with chronic reinnervation: large amplitude, long duration, polyphasic MUPs with reduced recruitment
quantitative_data.regions_with_denervation: 3 of 4 (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, with early lumbosacral changes)

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required tools (EMG/NCS, brain MRI, spine MRI, labs), 2 plausible red herrings (cervical spondylosis, remote CTS) require cross-modality synthesis to dismiss
metadata.notes: Moderate ALS case with bulbar-onset presentation complicated by concurrent cervical spondylosis on MRI. Key challenge is distinguishing myelopathic contribution from motor neuron disease — resolved by EMG demonstrating supra-cervical (bulbar) denervation.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. H is a 62-year-old right-handed woman who presents for neurological evaluation of an 8-month history of progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, and limb weakness. She initially noticed that her speech was becoming slurred and quieter approximately 8 months ago, which she initially attributed to fatigue. Over the following months, her speech worsened and she began having difficulty swallowing solid foods, requiring her to cut food into smaller pieces. She has had several episodes of coughing and choking while eating, particularly with thin liquids. Her husband noted that her voice has taken on a nasal quality and that she occasionally has uncontrollable laughing or crying that seems out of proportion to the situation.

Approximately 6 months ago, she noticed progressive bilateral arm weakness, initially affecting her left hand more than her right. She has difficulty buttoning shirts, opening jars, and holding a pen for extended periods. Over the past 3-4 months, she has also noticed bilateral leg weakness with difficulty climbing stairs and rising from low chairs. She denies any sensory symptoms, bladder or bowel dysfunction, or diplopia. She has noticed twitching in her tongue and arms.

Her primary care physician referred her for neurological evaluation. She has no significant family history of neurodegenerative disease and no toxic exposures. Review of systems is otherwise negative.

neurological_exam.additional: Fasciculations visible in tongue, bilateral deltoids, and left thenar eminence. No rash. Bulbar findings include dysarthria with palatal weakness and tongue fasciculations.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose-finger mildly dysmetric bilaterally, consistent with weakness. Heel-shin intact. Rapid alternating movements slowed.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: visual fields full bilaterally. CN III/IV/VI: extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus. CN V: facial sensation intact. CN VII: mild bilateral facial weakness. CN IX/X: palatal elevation asymmetric (left lower), gag reflex reduced bilaterally. CN XI: sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 4/5 bilaterally. CN XII: tongue atrophy noted bilaterally with visible fasciculations at rest, deviation to left on protrusion.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait slightly spastic, mildly wide-based. Tandem gait impaired. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Speech is mildly dysarthric with nasal quality and reduced volume. Articulation impaired on rapid alternating speech. Language comprehension intact. Mild emotional lability noted — patient tearful when describing symptoms.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral arm weakness: deltoids 4/5, biceps 4+/5, triceps 4/5, wrist extensors 4/5 bilaterally. Intrinsic hand muscles 4-/5 right, 3+/5 left. Visible fasciculations in bilateral upper extremity proximal muscles. Lower extremities: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally, quadriceps 4+/5, hamstrings 4+/5, ankle dorsiflexors 4/5, plantar flexors 4/5. No significant lower extremity atrophy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 3+ bilaterally, triceps 3+ bilaterally. Knee jerks 3+ bilaterally, ankle jerks 3+ bilaterally. Jaw jerk brisk. Plantar responses extensor bilaterally (Babinski present). Hoffman sign positive bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception intact throughout. No sensory level.
